name: The sea at night, from orbit
title: Night lights along the Mediterranean, from Spain to Libya
about: The lights of the coasts from Spain to Italy and from Algeria to Libya, photographed from the International Space Station on 23 September 2024.
why: The sea is drawn only by the people around it: Braudel's thousand things, as a thousand lights. It is the one picture here that shows the whole sea at once.

name: Sicily and Malta, from the Shuttle
title: Sicily and Malta, from Space Shuttle Endeavour
about: A view to the south from Space Shuttle Endeavour, April 2001: the whole triangle of Sicily, with Malta below it.
why: The text says Sicily is a triangle: here it is, with its outline as clear as the shape in the table, and Malta, the next table's most crowded island, at its foot.

name: Etna's plume
title: Etna's plume, Sicily
about: Steam blowing south from Etna's snowy summit, seen from Space Shuttle Endeavour in March 1994.
why: The row ends with Etna, 3,340 m: the picture is its highest point, alive.

name: Palermo cathedral, about 1900
title: Palermo. Cattedrale
about: A photochrom of about 1890 to 1900: a black and white negative printed in colour by the Photoglob company of Zürich.
why: Sicily from the ground, a century ago; better kept for “What the world keeps”, since Arab-Norman Palermo is a World Heritage site.

group: Twenty-two islands, each with its shape
name: The dolphins of Knossos
title: Dauphins de knossos
about: The dolphin fresco of the palace of Knossos, in Crete, as shown at the palace today (photograph of 2010). The Minoans painted it about three and a half thousand years ago.
why: Ramondino sees islands shaped like dolphins; the oldest dolphins of the Mediterranean were painted on an island. It is also the Minoan source of the design post.

group: Twenty-two islands, each with its shape
name: The whole of Crete, from Skylab
title: The whole island of Crete, from Skylab
about: Crete in one cloudless frame, photographed by the crew of Skylab on 22 June 1973.
why: An island seen as a shape and nothing else: what the shape nanoplots draw.

name: Lemnos, in Piri Reis's Book of the Sea
title: Piri Reis - Map of the Island of Lemnos - Walters W65847A - Full Page
when: a copy of the late 17th century
about: A page of the Kitab-ı Bahriye, the book of the sea of the Ottoman admiral Piri Reis, in a later copy at the Walters Art Museum: Lemnos, with rhumb lines and compass roses.
why: One island, alone, filling its page: the illusion the quote names, drawn five centuries ago, and the ancestor of the shape nanoplot. It is also the isolario direction of the design.

name: Buondelmonti's book of islands
title: Liber Insularum Archipelagi by Cristoforo Buondelmonti
about: Pages of Cristoforo Buondelmonti's Liber insularum Archipelagi, the book of the Aegean islands he wrote in 1420, one island per page.
why: The first of the island books: the same idea as the Piri Reis page, older; one of the two, not both.

group: All 195: rocks that only just have a name
name: Strombolicchio
title: Strombolicchio (tiny Stromboli)
about: The rock of Strombolicchio, with its lighthouse, off Stromboli, in the Aeolian Islands. A photograph shared on Flickr.
why: The story's lede promises “rocks that only just have a name”: this is one, an island that is a rock, a lighthouse and nothing else.

group: All 195: rocks that only just have a name
name: The Rabbit Island, Lampedusa
title: Isola dei Conigli a Lampedusa
about: The Isola dei Conigli, a small island off Lampedusa, and its bay. A photograph shared on Flickr.
why: Lampedusa is one of the two small islands with an airport; but a beach picture fits the last section better.

name: Kalymnos, in Piri Reis's Book of the Sea
title: Piri Reis - Map of the Island of Kalimnos - Walters W65888A - Full Page
when: a copy of the late 17th century
about: Another page of Piri Reis's Kitab-ı Bahriye (Walters Art Museum copy): the island of Kalymnos, in the Dodecanese, as an Ottoman sailor needed to know it.
why: A Greek island seen by an Ottoman admiral: the crossroads in one page. If Lemnos goes in “At the same scale”, this is the same book, so one of the two.

name: Venice, in Bordone's book of islands
title: 1528 - Bordone - Vinegia
about: The map of Venice in Benedetto Bordone's book of islands, printed in Venice in 1528.
why: Venice ruled Crete, Corfu and Cyprus for centuries; its own book of islands opens with Venice itself, a city on islands.

name: The Grand Harbour of Valletta, about 1900
title: Gezicht op de Grand Harbour in Valletta Malta, Grand Harbour (titel op object), RP-F-F01141-L
about: A print of about 1900 in the Rijksmuseum: the Grand Harbour of Valletta, Malta.
why: The harbour of the Knights, then of the British: Malta changed rulers more often than most.

name: Valletta's Royal Opera House, about 1900
title: Malta. Teatro Reale
about: A photochrom of the Teatro Reale of Valletta, built under British rule.
why: The rulers' buildings; but the harbour tells it better.

name: The stair of Santa Maria del Monte, Caltagirone
title: Scalinata di Santa Maria del Monte (Caltagirone) 22 12 2024 01
about: The 142 steps of the stair of Santa Maria del Monte, faced with maiolica, photographed in December 2024 and given to the public domain.
why: Caltagirone is one of the eight late Baroque towns of the Val di Noto, the example in the text; and its maiolica is a source of the design.

name: The Franciscans' pharmacy in Ragusa, about 1900
title: Cortile della farmacia de Franciscani, Ragusa, Sicily, Italy
about: A photochrom of a cloister courtyard in Ragusa, Sicily, with two friars.
why: Ragusa is another town of the Val di Noto; a quieter, older view.

name: Palermo cathedral, about 1900
title: Palermo. Cattedrale
about: The photochrom of the first group: the cathedral of Palermo.
why: Part of Arab-Norman Palermo, a World Heritage property since 2015; the crossroads of rulers in stone.

name: A luzzu in Malta
title: Reflections
about: The bright hull of a luzzu, a Maltese fishing boat, and its reflection in the harbour water. A photograph shared on Flickr.
why: Work at sea today, on the most crowded island; and the luzzu is a source of the design, whose colours told where a boat was from.

name: The fisherman of Akrotiri
title: Fresco of a fisherman, Akrotiri, Greece
about: A young fisherman holding two strings of fish: a fresco of Akrotiri, on Thera (Santorini), of about 1600 to 1500 BC.
why: The same work, three and a half thousand years earlier: a strong pair with the luzzu, if the section takes two.

name: Malta's custom house and landing place, about 1900
title: Gezicht op kust van Malta met steiger en douanegebouw Malta. Custom house and landing place (titel op object), RP-F-F01141-FI
about: A print of about 1900 in the Rijksmuseum: the custom house and the landing stage on the coast of Malta.
why: Trade and customs, the old work of a harbour; better for “Getting there”.

name: Capri's harbour, about 1880
title: Sommer, Giorgio (1834-1914) - n. 3142 - Capri, Marina - (ca. 1880)
about: Giorgio Sommer's photograph of the Marina of Capri, about 1880, with a steamship at anchor.
why: Anedda's first lesson in one picture: the only way off is the ship. The table then shows how the plane took over.

name: Capri's harbour town, about 1900
title: The town, Capri Island, Italy
about: A photochrom of the town and harbour of Capri, with boats drawn up on the water.
why: The same harbour twenty years later, in colour: one Capri, not both.

name: Malta's landing place, about 1900
title: Gezicht op kust van Malta met steiger en douanegebouw Malta. Custom house and landing place (titel op object), RP-F-F01141-FI
about: The Rijksmuseum print of the custom house and landing stage of Malta.
why: Where travellers came ashore, before the planes of the table.

name: Lussinpiccolo, about 1900
title: Lussin-Piccolo (i.e, Lussinpiccolo), general view, Istria, Austro-Hungary
about: A photochrom of Lussinpiccolo, today Mali Lošinj, on the island of Lošinj, next to Cres, when it was part of Austria-Hungary.
why: The text names Cres and Krk as the coolest in winter, when the bora blows: this is their neighbour, a century ago. Mali Lošinj is in the story's data too.

name: Pontikonisi, Corfu, about 1900
title: Corfoù. Pontikonisi LCCN2017658116
about: A photochrom of Pontikonisi, the islet off Corfu, in a calm sea.
why: The Ionian in summer stillness: the other face of the winds.

name: The water of Favignana
title: Water at Favignana Island, Sicily (Italy)
about: Clear shallow water and wild fennel on the coast of Favignana, in the Egadi Islands, west of Sicily. A photograph shared on Flickr.
why: The sea at its warmest, 26 to 28 °C in the south in August; today's colour against the old prints.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Rabbit Beach, Lampedusa
title: Lampedusa Rabbit beach - panoramio
about: The beach of the Isola dei Conigli, Lampedusa, photographed in August (Panoramio, on Wikimedia Commons).
why: A beach for the section that ends with one, on one of the small islands that have an airport.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Stromboli erupting
title: Stromboli Eruption
about: An eruption of Stromboli at night, photographed in 1980.
why: Something to see at night: a volcano that is almost always erupting.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: The Blue Grotto, Capri, about 1900
title: Blue grotto, Capri Island, Italy-LCCN2001700774
about: A photochrom of the Blue Grotto of Capri, with a boatman.
why: The most famous thing to see on an island, already a postcard in 1900.

name: A page of Buondelmonti's book of islands
title: 2012 NYR 02622 0155 000(buondelmonti cristoforo liber insularum archipelagi illuminated manusc)
about: An illuminated manuscript of Buondelmonti's Liber insularum Archipelagi, as photographed for a Christie's sale in 2012.
why: Matvejević's Isolario follows these books; but the section is a list of books, and may need no picture.

name: The Aegean by moonlight, from orbit
title: Night view over the Aegean Sea toward Greece
about: Looking south from over Romania across the Aegean to Greece, on a night with a moon: Thessaloniki near the centre, the larger glow of Athens on the left, Skopje below.
why: The same idea as the lights from orbit, but the moon lights the water, so the coasts and the islands of the Aegean read clearly: the sea is a shape, not only a dark gap.

name: Italy and all of Sicily, at night
title: Night image of most of Italy and all of Sicily
about: Most of Italy and the whole of Sicily, outlined by their lights; Rome and Naples near the centre, the Adriatic on the right.
why: The clearest coastline of the night pictures, and the story's first island, Sicily, whole, already in the opening picture.

name: Southern Italy and Sicily, south at the top
title: Night view over southern Italy
about: The boot and Sicily at night, photographed with south at the top of the picture.
why: Upside down, as al-Idrisi drew the world for Roger II in Palermo (in To read more): an opening that asks the reader to look at the sea from the other shore.

name: The whole sea, from the night lights of 2012
title: Black Marble: Africa, Europe and the Middle East
about: A composite of the night lights of Europe, Africa and the Middle East, from the Suomi NPP satellite's day-night band, laid over the Blue Marble.
why: The only picture where the whole Mediterranean is one dark shape ringed by lights; small on a phone, so best large, at the very top.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Cala Goloritzé, Sardinia
title: Cala Goloritze Sardegna
about: The view down to Cala Goloritzé, on the east coast of Sardinia, with its spire of rock in the sea.
why: Sardinia's beach, seen from the path down: a beach you reach on foot, through the macchia.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Elafonissi, Crete
title: Elafonissi, Chania, Greece
about: The beach of Elafonissi, in the far south-west of Crete, with shallow water and umbrellas of reed.
why: Crete's beach, crowded, as a beach is in the summer of the story's climate table.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Cala Macarella, Menorca
title: Cala Macarella
about: A small cove of Menorca between pines and white rock, with turquoise water.
why: The Balearics' beach, and the colour of the shallow sea that Vitali's palette took.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Pastizzi and Kinnie, Malta
title: Cheese pastizzi and Kinnie
about: A cheese pastizz in its paper and a bottle of Kinnie, Malta's bitter orange soda.
why: A taste, not a view: the one picture here that is food, for the taste of each island.

group: Something to see, a beach, a taste
name: Ħaġar Qim, Malta
title: Complejo de Ħaġar Qim, isla de Malta
about: A passage between the stones of the megalithic temple of Ħaġar Qim, under its protective tent.
why: A thing to see, and one of Malta's temples in the story's world heritage table.

name: Al-Idrisi's map, south at the top
title: Tabula Rogeriana, upside down
about: The world map of al-Idrisi's atlas, made in Palermo for Roger II of Sicily, in a copy with the names in Latin script, turned so north is up.
why: The book of a geographer at the court of Sicily: to read more begins on the story's first island, eight centuries ago.

name: The Carta Pisana
title: Carta Pisana
about: The oldest known portolan chart, found in Pisa: the whole Mediterranean and the Black Sea, on a single skin; now at the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
why: The sea before the isolari: the chart that every book of islands came after.

name: Fernand Braudel
title: Fernand Braudel (1902-1985)
about: A portrait of the historian; the file's page dates it to 1945, when he was a prisoner of war at Oflag X-C, near Lübeck.
why: The author of the story's first quote, who wrote much of The Mediterranean as a prisoner of war: a face for To read more.

name: A luzzu in Marsaxlokk, on blue water
title: Marsaxlokk Boat
